R02-A-01: It is natural to think of seeing as a kind of recording. Light enters the eye, an image forms on the retina, and the brain, like a careful clerk, reads off what is there. The picture is attractive because it matches how perception feels: effortless, immediate, and apparently free of any contribution from the perceiver. Yet the retinal image is a poor document: it is upside down, flat, constantly jittering with the movements of the eye, and interrupted by a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina. Above all, it is ambiguous, in the sense that a small image on the retina could be a small object nearby or a large one far away; a patch of dim grey could be a dark surface in bright light or a pale surface in shadow. The eye, in short, delivers considerably less information than we ordinarily experience ourselves as seeing. For this reason many students of vision have preferred to describe perception as a form of inference. The brain, on this account, treats the incoming signal as evidence and settles on the interpretation that best explains it, given what it has learned about how the world usually is. Light tends to come from above, so a disc shaded darker at the bottom is seen as a bump and the same disc turned over as a dent. Objects tend to keep their size, so a person walking away is seen as receding rather than shrinking. These are not conclusions we reach; they are conclusions reached on our behalf, before anything is presented to awareness. The word 'inference' invites an obvious objection: if perception is a guess shaped by expectation, why do we not simply see whatever we expect? The answer is that the guess is tightly disciplined by the evidence, and that the expectations doing the work are of a peculiar kind. They are not the beliefs we hold and can revise in conversation, but assumptions built up over a lifetime of looking, and perhaps over the history of the species. This is why many visual illusions survive full knowledge of the trick. A viewer who has measured two lines and found them equal will still see one as longer; what she knows and what she sees have been settled by different processes. It would be a mistake, then, to conclude that perception is unreliable because it is inferential. The assumptions it relies on are mostly true of the environments in which they were formed, which is why they so rarely mislead us outside the laboratory, where illusions are carefully built to exploit them. What the inferential view really overturns is not our trust in the senses but the idea that seeing is passive. Every glance is a small act of interpretation, and its seeming effortlessness is the mark of how well the work is done, not evidence that no work is being done.
R02-A-02: Most people believe that anything sufficiently striking will catch their eye. If a person in a gorilla suit walked through a game of catch we were watching, we assume we would notice. A well-known series of experiments suggests otherwise. When viewers are asked to count the passes made by one team in a short video, a large share of them fail to see an unexpected figure stroll through the middle of the scene, even when it pauses to face the camera. Asked afterwards, many insist that nothing unusual happened, and some are indignant when the recording is replayed. The phenomenon, usually called inattentional blindness, is easy to misread as a failure of the eyes. It is not, or at least not in any sense that an optician could detect: the light from the unexpected figure reaches the retina as surely as the light from the ball. What fails is the selection that decides which parts of the scene will be built into conscious experience. Attention is not a spotlight that merely brightens what we are looking at; it is closer to a gate, and what does not pass through the gate is not dimly seen but, for practical purposes, not seen at all. The finding matters less because of its surprise value than because of the confidence it exposes. We are poor judges of what we would notice, because the things we miss leave no trace in experience from which we could learn that we missed them. Ordinary experience, which might be expected to correct our overconfidence, cannot do so, because an occasion on which we failed to notice something is, from the inside, indistinguishable from an occasion on which there was nothing to notice. A driver who looks at a junction while thinking about something else may have no sense that a cyclist was in view. Afterwards he will report, quite sincerely, that the cyclist came from nowhere. His honesty is not in question; his access to his own lapse is. This should not be taken to mean that attention is simply defective. A mind that admitted everything in the visual field to awareness would be overwhelmed, unable to follow the ball, read a page or hold a conversation in a crowded room. Selectivity is the price of focus, and on most days, when little that we fail to notice turns out to matter, the price is low. The lesson is narrower and more practical: where the cost of missing something is high, we should not rely on the conviction that we would have seen it, and should instead design tasks, roads and warning signals on the assumption that attention is already spoken for.
R02-A-03: Ask people where they were when they heard of some great public shock, an assassination, a disaster broadcast live, the sudden death of a famous figure, and many will answer at once and in detail. They remember the room, who told them, what they were holding, the first thing they said. Such recollections have been called flashbulb memories, the name suggesting that a moment of intense feeling exposes the scene, as a flash exposes film, and fixes it for good. The people who hold them are rarely in doubt. Of all their memories, these seem the least likely to be wrong. The difficulty is that when such memories have been checked, they have often turned out to be wrong in exactly the ways ordinary memories are. Researchers have questioned people within a day or two of a widely reported event and then again months or years later. The later accounts frequently differ from the earlier ones, sometimes in small particulars and sometimes wholesale: a person who first wrote that she heard the news from a colleague at work later describes, with complete assurance, watching it on television at home. Confronted with her own earlier account, she may concede that she wrote it while continuing to feel that her present memory is the true one. What sets these memories apart, then, is not their accuracy but the confidence and vividness with which they are held; in these memories, conviction and correctness have come apart. One explanation is that the events are rehearsed endlessly. They are discussed with friends, revisited in anniversary broadcasts and retold until the story has a familiar shape. Each retelling is less a replay than a reconstruction, and the most recent reconstruction is the one that feels like the original. Emotion contributes too, but perhaps less to the record than to the sense of its importance: a moment that mattered seems as though it must have been remembered faithfully. None of this means that strong feeling has no effect on memory. People rarely forget that the event happened, and there is reason to think that emotion sharpens memory for whatever is central to an experience while letting the periphery blur. The trouble is that the details we are proudest of recalling, the room, the messenger, the coffee cup, are precisely the peripheral ones. The practical lesson extends well beyond public events. Wherever memory is used as evidence, the vividness of a recollection and the certainty of the person reporting it are weaker guides to its truth than we are inclined to believe.
R02-A-04: We tend to speak of forgetting as a failure, the mind's equivalent of a leaking roof: students blame it for poor marks, older people fear it as a sign of decline, and whole industries promise to reduce it. Behind these attitudes lies an assumption that an ideal memory would keep everything. Even our vocabulary betrays the attitude, since we speak of 'losing' a memory as though it were a possession that had slipped out of a pocket. It is worth asking whether the assumption behind such talk is true. Consider what such a memory would be like to live with. Every time you parked your car, you would recall not only today's space but every space you had ever used, each with equal force. Every time you met a friend, you would be confronted with each version of her face across the years. The problem would not be a shortage of information but a surplus of it, because the memory you needed would be buried among the memories you did not. Some people who report unusually complete recall of their own lives describe the gift less as a pleasure than as a burden, a past that will not stay in the past. Seen in this light, much forgetting looks less like decay than like editing. Memories that are rarely used become harder to reach, while those that are used often stay accessible, and the effect is less a loss than a reordering of priorities. This is roughly what a sensible filing system would do: it would keep the files you consult near at hand and move the rest to the back, on the reasonable bet that the past use of a memory predicts its future use. Some evidence even suggests that recalling one memory actively suppresses its competitors, so that using your new phone number makes the old one fade faster. This argument has limits, and it is easy to push it too far, for not all forgetting is useful: the losses caused by brain injury or dementia are not editing but damage, and nothing said here makes them less painful. Nor does a system that is well designed on average serve every individual case: the name you cannot recall at an important meeting is a real cost, even if it is the price of a sensible policy. The point is only that the capacity to forget is part of what makes memory useful, not simply a flaw in it. A memory that never let go would be a worse memory, not a better one.
R02-A-05: A familiar demonstration from the study of chess runs as follows. A position from a real game is shown for a few seconds and then removed, and players are asked to reconstruct it on an empty board. Strong players replace most of the pieces correctly, while novices manage only a handful, and the obvious conclusion is that strong players simply have better memories. The less obvious and more instructive part of the demonstration comes next. When the same pieces are scattered at random, in arrangements that could never arise in play, the masters' advantage largely disappears, and they do little better than beginners. What the masters possess, then, is not a larger store for holding pieces but a different way of seeing them. Years of play have given them a vocabulary of familiar configurations, a castled king with its pawns in front, a bishop aimed down a long diagonal, and they take in a position as a few such units rather than as two dozen separate pieces. A novice looking at the same board sees wood on squares. The master sees a situation, and often, before any conscious calculation has begun, a sense of what the situation calls for. Similar observations have been made in fields as different as radiology, birdwatching and the reading of geological maps, where experienced specialists frequently report knowing that something is wrong with an image within a second or two, before they can say what it is. The birdwatcher who names a distant species from the way it flies, long before any marking can be made out, is drawing on the same resource. It is tempting to describe this as intuition, as though it were a mysterious faculty standing apart from knowledge. It is better described as knowledge that has been absorbed into perception, so that it no longer needs to be consulted, because it shapes what is seen in the first place. This view has practical consequences, though they are easily overstated. If expertise lies partly in the eye, it cannot be fully transmitted by rules and explanations; the learner has to look at a great many cases, with feedback, until the patterns become visible. But perception is not the whole of expertise. Masters still calculate, and careful specialists still check their first impressions, because a pattern that is recognised instantly can also be misrecognised instantly. The trained eye is fast and usually right within the territory that trained it, and that qualification matters: presented with a case unlike those it has learned from, its speed becomes a liability rather than an asset.
R02-A-06: There is a small puzzle about time that most people have noticed without ever stating it. A week spent travelling somewhere new seems to vanish while it is happening, so that there is never enough of it; yet once the traveller is home, the same week looks enormous, crowded with places and faces, as if it had lasted a month. A week at a familiar desk behaves in the opposite way. It drags while it is lived, each afternoon longer than the last, and then collapses in memory into a single grey item that seems to have taken no time at all. The puzzle dissolves once we accept that we judge duration in two quite different ways. While an interval is passing, our sense of its length depends largely on how much attention we pay to time itself: boredom draws attention to the clock and stretches the hour, while absorption draws it away and the hour shrinks. Looking back, however, we have no clock to consult. We estimate how long a period lasted from what it left behind, and a period that left many distinct memories is judged to have been long. Novelty therefore works in opposite directions on the two judgements, shortening the interval as experienced and lengthening it as remembered. This distinction sheds light on a complaint that becomes common in middle age, that the years go faster than they used to. The complaint is almost always retrospective. Few people find that a particular afternoon passes faster at fifty than at fifteen; what they find is that last year, viewed as a whole, seems to have been brief. If remembered duration tracks the number of distinct memories, the explanation is not far to seek, since adult life is more routine than youth, with fewer firsts, and a year of repeated weeks leaves less behind to measure it by. The account is persuasive, but it should be held loosely. It is unlikely that a single factor explains how time seems at every age, and other changes, in health, in responsibility, in how far ahead people habitually plan, probably play a part. Still less does it follow, as some cheerful advice suggests, that one can lengthen a life simply by filling it with novelty. A crowded year may indeed look longer in retrospect, but it will feel shorter while it is lived, and there is no obvious reason to prefer one of these measures over the other. What the distinction teaches is not a technique for buying time but a caution against speaking of how long something 'really' felt, as though there were only one answer.
R02-A-07: For much of its short history as a subject of research, the wandering mind was treated as noise. Participants in experiments were supposed to attend to the task in front of them, and the moments when their thoughts drifted to lunch or to an argument with a sibling were lapses to be minimised or averaged away. When researchers began to study these lapses directly, by interrupting people at random moments in their day and asking what they had been thinking about, the first surprise was how common the lapses were. The method had the merit of catching thought in the act, before the thinker had time to tidy it into a more respectable account of where her attention had been. A considerable part of waking thought, it turned out, is about something other than what the thinker is doing. Two quite different interpretations of this finding have since competed. On the first, mind wandering is a failure of control: it is associated with errors in reading and driving, with poorer performance on tests of sustained attention and, in some studies, with lower reported mood at the moment of wandering. The mind that drifts is the mind that has lost its grip, and the remedy is training in attention. On the second interpretation, these costs are real but partial, and they ignore what the drifting mind is actually doing. Much wandering thought is directed at the future, at plans, rehearsals of conversations and the weighing of unfinished business, and some of the solutions that arrive unbidden in the shower or on a walk may owe something to the same process. On this view the mind that drifts is not idle but working on a different problem, one it has judged, so to speak, more pressing than the task at hand. Each interpretation, I think, makes the same mistake, which is to speak of mind wandering as though it were one thing with one value. The evidence for costs comes largely from tasks that demand continuous attention, where any lapse is damaging by design, while the evidence for benefits comes largely from situations in which the external task is undemanding, so that little is lost by leaving it. Tasks of the first kind are chosen precisely because they make lapses easy to count, and situations of the second kind because they leave room for thought. It is hardly surprising that the two literatures reach different verdicts, since they are, for the most part, looking at different occasions. Nor does the link with low mood settle the matter. A person who is worried is likely both to feel worse and to find his thoughts pulled towards his worries, so that wandering may be as much a symptom of unhappiness as its cause. A more useful question is not whether the mind should wander but when, and with what awareness. Drifting during a lecture one has chosen to attend is a cost; drifting while washing dishes may be a free opportunity to think. There also seems to be a real difference between thought that slips away unnoticed and thought that is allowed to roam, as when a person deliberately sets a problem aside and lets her attention go where it will. The second kind is under a loose but genuine control, since the person can notice it and call it back. If this is right, the goal of training attention should not be to abolish wandering, an aim that is probably unachievable and possibly harmful, but to make wandering more visible to the wanderer, so that she can tell which kind of occasion she is in.
R02-A-08: In most schools a test is understood as a thermometer. It is applied at the end of a period of learning to find out how much has been learned, and like a thermometer it is supposed to leave the thing it measures unchanged. The understanding is so familiar that it seldom occurs to anyone that it might be false. Yet one of the more robust findings in the psychology of memory is that the act of retrieving something from memory is not a neutral reading: it changes the memory, and generally strengthens it, so that material which has been recalled once is more likely to be recalled again than material which has merely been seen again. The contrast is clearest when the two activities are set against each other. Suppose two groups of students study the same passage, after which one group rereads it while the other closes the book and writes down whatever it can remember. The design holds constant both the material and the time spent on it, so that the only difference between the groups is whether they looked at the passage again or tried to bring it back unaided. Tested a few minutes later, the rereaders often do as well or better; tested a week later, the group that practised recall tends to remember considerably more. The advantage of retrieval, in other words, is easily hidden by the timing of the measurement, which may be one reason why it was overlooked for so long by teachers and students alike. What is more striking is how little the students themselves sense any of this. Asked to predict their own performance, rereaders tend to be the more confident group. Rereading produces a feeling of fluency, in which the sentences are familiar and slide past easily, and ease of processing is readily mistaken for mastery. Attempting recall produces the opposite feeling, since it is effortful, it exposes gaps and it is often unpleasant, which is presumably why students left to themselves so rarely choose it. Teachers are not immune to the same illusion, since a class that has just reread its notes looks, and feels, better prepared than one that has just struggled to recall them. The method that feels like learning and the method that produces it are, at least here, not the same, and the lesson generalises uncomfortably: a learner's own sense of how well a session went is an unreliable guide to how much it achieved. It would be easy to draw from all this a crude conclusion, that schools should simply test more, but the finding does not support it. What strengthens memory is the effort of retrieval, not the apparatus of examination, and the apparatus can work against the effort. A high-stakes test that provokes anxiety, or that is followed by no feedback, may teach students little except to fear tests, and a wrong answer recalled confidently and never corrected may itself be strengthened. The useful practice is humbler than the word 'test' suggests: it consists of frequent, low-stakes attempts to recall, each followed by a chance to check, built into ordinary study. None of this requires abolishing examinations, which serve purposes of certification that have little to do with memory; it requires only that they not be mistaken for the whole of what testing can do. Understood in this way, the thermometer turns out to be one of the more effective means of raising the temperature it was meant only to record.
